Optical flow estimation is a fundamental computer vision task that requires
minimal supervision. In recent years, self-supervised flow estimation has been
successful, with techniques like correlation-based and photometric methods
achieving high accuracy. However, these methods struggle with occlusions,
representing a significant obstacle to accurate flow estimation. In this work, a
novel perspective on flow estimation is presented, driven by a simplified
assumption that each pixel can be divided into two parts: a non-occluded part
with a unique motion vector and an occluded part with undetermined motion.
This two-component model is then applied to a list-discussion framework that
efficiently handles occlusions by leveraging the uniqueness of motion vectors.
The approach is further extended to a dense flow estimation technique based
on a minimization problem, solved using a novel spatial-aware smoothness term.
The proposed method and its variants are extensively evaluated on seven public
datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results or comparable performance to the
current top-ranking methods, particularly excelling in scenes with occlusions.
Furthermore, qualitative flow maps illustrate the ability of the technique to
accurately capture complex scenes with occlusions, thereby demonstrating the
method's effectiveness in handling this common vision challenge. Implementation
details, experimental settings, and code are available at

By modifying the QCD Lagrangian to account for the effects of a strong magnetic field and using a mean-field approximation, we have derived a modified mass term for quarks and obtained a modified equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter under strong magnetic fields. Our research proves that any E2F cubic graph has a Hamiltonian cycle and includes all previously known results on Hamiltonian cycles within the class of E2F cubic graphs. Additionally, we provide an infinite number of non-isomorphic constructions for E2F cubic graphs, demonstrating that no algorithm can determine if a given cubic graph is E2F in polynomial time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the problem of determining if a given cubic graph is E2F is equivalent to the Hamiltonian cycle problem and can be solved in pseudo-polynomial time. Moreover, we show that every E2F cubic graph contains a Hamiltonian cycle that can be found in pseudo-polynomial time, and finally, we show that the class of E2F cubic graphs includes all Hamiltonian cubic graphs. All previous known results on Hamiltonian cycles within the class of E2F cubic graphs, including those found in the literature, can be found in the appendix of this research. We also introduce the concept of odd-2-factorable (O2F) cubic graphs and provide an infinite number of non-isomorphic constructions for O2F cubic graphs, as well as proving that no algorithm can determine if a given cubic graph is odd-2F in polynomial time. System call filtering is a critical security feature that enables applications to isolate from the system they're running on. Although various techniques filter system calls for applications written in low-level programming languages like C and Java, there's a notable absence of solutions for interpreted languages like PHP and Python. In order to address this issue for widely-used web applications, a novel approach called Timeloops has been developed, incorporating system call filtering into PHP and Python frameworks via lightweight, trusted code. In order to mitigate potential delays caused by frequent system call filtering, Timeloops employs an innovative technique called Coarse-Grained All-Purpose Permission Policies, granting applications unrestricted access to system calls for a brief period before isolating them following the completion of their execution. In order to minimize security risks, a sophisticated mechanism called Dynamic System Call Whitelisting has been developed, allowing administrators to define customizable lists of system calls that applications can use. In order to evaluate the performance, security, and convenience of Timeloops, a comprehensive assessment was conducted, comparing the feature against alternative Linux security modules using real-world PHP and Python workloads. We develop a novel algorithm for detecting and tracking hidden targets in a surveillance network. The algorithm processes data from cameras with limited fields of view to determine the likelihood of objects being within their viewing area. We used a chance-constrained formulation to express the hidden target detection problem, but this approach is computationally intensive due to the limited sensor data. To address this challenge, we reframe the algorithm as a multiple-choice knapsack problem, significantly reducing its computational complexity. The resulting algorithm exhibits improved computational efficiency, particularly when tracking undetected targets. We tested and validated our algorithm through simulations and real-world applications, including a case study of a security system at an airport terminal. The results showed our algorithm provides the best solution among various optimization methods in terms of both solution quality and computational time. The code for our algorithm is available on https://github.com/TargetDetectionTracker. The data used in the case study can be found on https://github.com/TargetDetectionTracker/Data. We examine a recent observability inequality for a one-dimensional damped wave system to derive a decay rate of $O(e^{AT})$ in time $T$, where $A$ is a constant with specific value restrictions. This observability measure can be adapted to manage population growth or decline in mathematical models, particularly those featuring the spread of a species, as seen in the example provided. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of this method to ensure that a population model, featuring a growing or shrinking overall population, eventually converges to zero. Further, we outline the steps to extend this technique to a growing population model and provide the derivations for desired observability inequalities in the previous examples. Finally, we outline possible future directions for expanding on these methods, including the potential to combine these techniques with optimal control strategies. We analyze the underlying structure of soccer rewards by comparing the value of actions like committing a foul or the ball going out of bounds to the value of shooting on goal. Our research utilizes a hierarchical reinforcement learning model that breaks down the game into manageable components, allowing us to quantify the rewards for different actions and task priorities. Our findings show that the rewards for actions like the ball going out of bounds or a foul are around one-tenth of the reward for shooting on goal, with slightly higher value assigned to certain types of fouls committed in specific situations. Additionally, our model reveals that the rewards for actions are influenced by the phase of the game and the team's score, with a greater emphasis on defending in the latter stages of the game. Our approach also enables the incorporation of domain knowledge and improves the generalization of learned policies by constraining the rewards in a soccer-specific manner. Our trained agent demonstrates enhanced performance in comparison to a standard policy, particularly in high-stakes situations. We have investigated an asymmetric noisy voter model where two species can coexist and compete for space, and the competition between them follows a simple rule where each individual randomly chooses one other individual to copy, including the possibility of copying itself, although this last option is less probable. The model is noisy because some individuals fail to change their color after the random selection, known as the asymmetric conditional random edge (ACRE) dynamics. The model also allows for the removal of existing edges at a random rate, known as the erdos-renyi (ER) dynamics. We combined ACRE and ER dynamics to study the competitive process between the two species. The model can be studied through a simple mathematical approach that leads to the derivation of a set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) whose solutions reveal various possible outcomes, including the extinction of one species, the coexistence of both species, or the periodic oscillations of the species' proportions. The analysis of the ODEs also highlights the role of the model's parameters in determining the final results, as well as the significance of a specific ratio that serves as a indicator of the species' proportions in the coexistence phase. The study of the model's dynamics was further validated through numerical simulations. The coexistence ratio was found to exhibit a non-monotonic dependence on the asymmetry of the model, first increasing with increasing asymmetry before eventually decreasing. The model's dynamics were found to transition from a state of periodic oscillations to a state of permanent coexistence, conditional on the initial proportions of the two species. The study also revealed the existence of a threshold in the model's parameters above which the model's dynamics result in the extinction of one species. The model's dynamics were found to be influenced by the addition of random edge removals, resulting in the disintegration of the system within a finite time. The study of the model provides a framework that can be applied to a wide range of natural phenomena, including the spread of languages, the competition between different species of plants and animals, and the influence of social interactions on the spread of ideas and behaviors. The study also highlights the significance of considering the impact of random events on the dynamics of complex systems. The model's simplicity makes it an ideal tool for teaching students about the basic principles of dynamics and the impact of random events on complex systems. We present a comprehensive mathematical framework for analyzing the design of electrostatic phase plates in Scanning Electron Microscopes, consisting of a grid of filled and empty pixels that modulate the electron beam. This model allows us to calculate the precise effect that phase plate design has on the shape of the electron probe and current density within the specimen plane. By examining various pixel patterns, including square, circular, and hexagonal shapes, we can determine the ideal fill factor that produces the smallest probe size while also maximizing the current density within the specified plane. This approach is particularly useful for optimizing the performance of modern Spinning Disk Electron Microscopes equipped with a liquid crystal phase plate. By examining the probe shapes and current density distributions produced by different phase plate designs, particularly those with fill factors of 50% or less, we demonstrate the potential for these instruments to produce high-resolution images with large probe currents. This, in turn, enables the simultaneous acquisition of high-resolution images and low-loss electron energy loss spectra. We also investigate the limitations of phase plate design, including the minimum probe size achievable and the occurrence of satellite probes, which can arise from certain pixel patterns, particularly those with small fill factors. By carefully selecting the design of the phase plate, we can minimize these negative effects, ultimately allowing for the simultaneous acquisition of high-resolution images and energy loss spectra from the same region of interest. This represents a significant advancement in the capabilities of modern Electron Microscopes. Experimental verification of our predictions is demonstrated using a liquid crystal phase plate on a Spinning Disk Electron Microscope, with results showing excellent agreement between simulation and actual data. This includes accurate predictions of probe shapes and current density distributions produced by different phase plate designs, as well as the minimum probe size achievable and the corresponding fill factor required to produce probes with diameters less than 0.5 angstrom. Additionally, we provide a detailed examination of how varying the acceleration voltage affects the probe shape and current density within the specimen plane, along with a comprehensive analysis of how the probe shape changes with different fill factors, particularly at very low fill factors. We examine the stability of a solitary wave, initially present in the system, as it interacts with the third particle over time. Our research reveals that the presence of an anharmonic oscillator in the system leads to the loss of its orbital stability, resulting in the solitary wave breaking down into a series of solitons or waves with different velocities. Our approach also allows us to compare our results with existing harmonic models, revealing that the anharmonic potential accelerates the solitary wave's breakdown. Additionally, we find that in a system with an anharmonic potential, multiple solitary waves can coexist and interact, merging into larger solitary waves or dispersing into waves with varying speeds. We establish a key connection between the Galois module structure of a finite non-abelian extension of the rational numbers and the additive Galois module structure it occupies in the ring of Galois modules over the ring of integers. This additive Galois module ring contains the ring of Galois modules generated by the absolute Galois group of the rational numbers, and its structure near a particular composition law can be characterized using combinatorial group theory. This characterisation allows us to determine how the additive Galois module structure of a specific finite non-abelian extension, known as a wildly ramified extension, is configured. This adds to our previous research on abelian extensions and provides a suitable replacement for Descent's 1965 unconfirmed claims about the Galois module structure of these extensions. Additionally, this research paves the way for further investigation into the additive Galois module structure of all finite non-abelian extensions of the rational numbers. 

This article first outlines the necessary background on the additive Galois module structure of the absolute Galois group of the rational numbers and the ring of Galois modules it generates. It then delves into the specifics of a finite non-abelian extension, known as a wildly ramified extension, and explores the additive Galois module structure that this extension occupies in the ring of Galois modules. It also outlines the methodology used to determine the additive Galois module structure of these extensions and presents three possible composition law scenarios they can adhere to. Finally, it is worth noting that the research presented in this article remains purely theoretical in nature, given the limited understanding of the additive Galois module structure of the absolute Galois group of the rational numbers and the ring of Galois modules it generates. To discover a neutral long-lived particle at a collider, its decay length is a critical factor due to the diverse impact it has on our search approach, detector effects, and theoretical models that could give rise to such a particle. This study provides a comprehensive review of a neutral long-lived particle's effects on a collider's detector, the various search strategies employed, and the relevant theoretical contexts. We also outline future directions for research, particularly at the LHC and its proposed upgrades, as well as future colliders like the ILC, CLF, and SDC. Furthermore, we outline simulated search strategies for a neutral long-lived gluon or lepton and provide optimized decay length ranges that could lead to viable searches at the LHC, the 100 TeV LHC, the ILC, and the CLF. We also discuss the potential for a neutral long-lived particle to be detected through missing transverse energy, missing mass, or through the decay products it leaves behind in the detector, depending on its decay length and the collider in question. Additionally, we examine the potential for such a particle to be produced in Compton processes, photon-photon interactions, and in inelastic collisions at future colliders. If detected, a neutral long-lived particle could provide a rich source of information about the underlying physics, including, for instance, the mass scale of the particle, its decay width, its lifetime, the relevant production processes, as well as the underlying theories that could give rise to such a particle, such as additional scalar or vector fields, extra dimensions, or certain extensions of the standard model. If remains elusive, we discuss the potential for future colliders and detectors that could make such a discovery possible. We also outline the detection challenges posed by a neutral long-lived particle that could mimic background events or remain undetected in the collider's detector. We conclude by emphasizing the need for a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics and the relevant production and detection processes that could give rise to the discovery of a neutral long-lived particle at a collider. Understanding how word meanings change over time is crucial for developing effective and adaptable language models. Recent advances in modeling semantic change rely on a key assumption - the variance of contextual representations remains constant. However, our analysis reveals that contextual variance itself evolves, influencing the interpretation of semantic shifts, especially when analyzing polar words like ``good'' compared to more neutral words like "dog". We demonstrate that models failing to account for changing variance often misinterpret the structure of the vocabulary, leading to inconsistent representations and inaccurate predictions. Furthermore, we show that a simple, manually crafted approach that adapts contextual variance to historical data can mitigate these issues, leading to a more accurate model of semantic change, especially for words with extreme distributional properties. Despite its limitations, this approach provides a baseline for future work, given the restricted performance of current unsupervised techniques, according to our experiments on three historical datasets. A collaborative framework is proposed for image reconstruction, combining compressive sensing with a sparsity-promoting optimizer. The approach involves creating a flexible optimizer that can be configured to suit various images and sources, and has been successfully applied in a variety of image processing tasks including deblurring, super-resolution, and compressive photography. The core technique behind this framework is a weighted Toeplitz matrix design method, which minimizes the mutual coherence of the sensing matrix to enhance reconstruction performance. The method is further enhanced by integrating a post-reconstruction coherence-reduction step, resulting in an accelerated and more accurate reconstruction process. The technique has been tested under various conditions and its superiority established when compared to alternative methods, including the standard Toeplitz matrix and deep learning compressive sensing architectures. The resulting images from this technique demonstrate a significant improvement in both quantitative and qualitative metrics, as evidenced by PSNR, SSIM and perceptual analysis. Using archival data from Kepler, we have monitored the closest approach points of
twenty-one objects within the Kozai lid for a minimum of one hundred and seventy
days. We have detected the rotation periods of ten small planets or asteroids at
different orbital eccentricities and have found that their rotation speeds are
increasing over time as they near their closest approach to the host star. We have
also determined the detection efficiency for suitable asteroid shapes and sizes
and plan to continue studying these objects with ongoing and future telescopes. 
Although we initially expected the detected asteroids to have highly eccentric
rotation patterns similar to some of the previously discovered ones, our data show
that most of them have rotation patterns that are consistently accelerated. We have
also found that the rotation acceleration of the detected asteroids is linked to
their orbital eccentricities and suggest that they may have undergone similar
formation processes. We have further found that the minimum distance of the close
approach point marks the beginning of the acceleration of rotation speed and also
marks the point when temperature differences cause the surface of the asteroids
to heat up and cool down, causing their rotation speeds to accelerate and slow
down respectively. We have also determined that the rotation speed of the
detected asteroids remains constant when the orbital eccentricity is very low and
we have observed that the detected asteroids always complete a rotation on their
axis at least once before the close approach point, implying that they do not
have irregular rotation patterns. We have also found that the time it takes for
the surface temperature differences to accelerate or decelerate the rotation speed
of the detected asteroids to be at least two years or more and we have
conjectured that larger planets or asteroids with surface layers may have
rotation speeds that are consistently accelerated for a much longer period of time. 
We have also determined that the detected small planets or asteroids are within
the size range of one hundred to three hundred and fifty kilometers in diameter 
and we have further found that the detected small planets or asteroids have
surface temperatures that range from three hundred and fifty degrees Kelvin to 
seventy degrees Kelvin and we have also found that the minimum distance of the 
close approach point causes surface temperature differences of up to one hundred 
and fifty degrees Kelvin on the surface of the detected small planets or 
asteroids. We have also found that the time it takes for the surface temperature 
differences to accelerate or decelerate the rotation speed of the detected small

Animacy is a fundamental concept in psychology and philosophy that extends beyond binary categorizations of living versus non-living entities. Recent studies suggest a continuous framework for animacy, encompassing various degrees of agency and visual categorizability. Additionally, we demonstrate that the hypothesis of the existence of Landau-Siegel zeros is incompatible with the 2-part of the conjectural subconvexity estimate for these L-functions. Based on the analytics subconvexity, we can also exclude the possibility of Landau-Siegel zeros. We also discuss possible applications to automorphic forms of higher rank. Given the analyticity of certain Dirichlet L-value zeros and the repulsion of these zeros from the critical line, we can conclude that there are no Landau-Siegel zeros in that particular case. We anticipate that the 2-part of the analytic subconvexity conjecture for GL_2 also holds under certain level conditions, although this would follow from the broader context of the Langlands program. This presentation introduces the principles of Quantum Relational Hoare Logic (QRHL), 
a formal verification system designed to analyze the behavior of quantum programs. 
QRHL enables the specification and validation of the relationship between input and 
output data sets for quantum programs, utilizing a relational Hoare logic framework. 
Key features of this logic include: (1) a relational format for expressing input/output 
relationships that can be accurately reflected in output data sets, (2) a method to 
accurately assess the precision and coverage of these relationships, and (3) a method 
to efficiently update these relationships as new data becomes available. Furthermore, 
QRHL includes a set of predefined predicates that can be used to assess the precision 
and the coverage of these relationships, as well as various methods for updating and 
refining the relationships. These features collectively provide a precise and efficient 
method for validating the behavior of quantum programs in accordance with their 
intended purpose. This presentation also presents a sample application of QRHL in 
the context of a quantum machine learning algorithm designed to accurately identify 
members of a predefined set. This validation demonstrates the program's ability 
to efficiently learn from new data while accurately adhering to the predefined 
set guidelines, which is crucial for preventing overfitting and ensuring the 
program's reliability in unfamiliar situations. This development paves the way 
for a formal verification framework tailored for quantum programs with data sets 
as input and output, and paves the ground for a future verified quantum programming 
language that incorporates verifiable and reliable machine learning algorithms. 
This presentation is an extension of a presentation that was previously given 
at the 2023 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Functional Programming.

Recent close-quarters outbreaks in settings like public transportation, meeting rooms, and crowded restaurants have sparked interest in a new model that combines standard epidemiological methods with features specific to these isolated incidents. Known as the "super-spreader model," it diverges from traditional models by incorporating distinct infection dynamics within these enclosed spaces. In a new study, the model is applied to accommodate recent infections on buses in China, specifically in Hunan and Guangdong. By using the model in a multi-objective framework that incorporates data from various local authorities, the researchers are able to determine the most plausible infection scenarios for each bus incident. Furthermore, the model is validated through simulations that compare standard epidemiological methods with the super-spreader model, revealing that the latter more accurately estimates infection probabilities for the majority of bus passengers. Additionally, the model effectively accounts for varying levels of mask usage, with mask-wearers exhibiting reduced infection probabilities of 55-70% compared to non-mask-wearers. The research also explores the optimal seating arrangements to minimize infection risk on buses. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the versatility of the super-spreader model in adapting to new contexts and its potential for broad application in understanding and predicting the spread of infections within enclosed spaces. Systematic reviews of the literature through Google Scholar using relevant search terms were used to gather information on previous bus outbreaks in various countries, including but not limited to South Korea, Japan, Austria, and the United Kingdom. The research found that the model could be applied to bus incidents worldwide, with one exception being an incident in South Korea where the model overestimated the number of infections due to a unique combination of factors present on that particular bus. The model assumes that all bus passengers interact randomly with each other, which is deemed suitable given the short duration of bus journeys, with one study citing a notable example from Austria where interactions on a bus for just one minute were found to lead to infections among bus passengers. The research also highlights the limitations of the model by pointing out that it does not account for differences in ventilation on buses, with one study in Hunan, China revealing that buses with the best ventilation had infection rates 60-80% lower than buses with the worst ventilation. The study concludes by emphasizing the need for further research into the effects of ventilation on buses to improve the model, with potential applications including developing guidelines for optimal seating arrangements and ventilation systems on buses to minimize infection risk. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence enable models to make accurate predictions, though selecting the best model often becomes a challenging task due to the private nature of training data. We propose a novel, privacy-preserving framework to efficiently find the optimal model by reusing previously trained models, even when the original training data remains confidential. We demonstrate that traditional optimization techniques, such as grid search, are impractical in this setting due to their intensive computational requirements and data privacy violations. To address this issue, we develop a precision-guided method that leverages a precision distribution to guide model precision and train a final model using a small public dataset. We evaluate our framework in real-world settings, including a medical diagnosis application and a financial forecasting platform, and the results show that it achieves comparable performance to models trained on private data with significantly reduced computational costs. We open-source our framework at https://precisefm.github.io/. We also publish our replication packages at https://github.com/precisefm/code and https://github.com/precisefm/data. We intend to further improve our framework based on feedback from the community. We look forward to collaborating with researchers and practitioners who share our interest in addressing the challenges associated with model evaluation and hyperparameter tuning in real-world settings. The APOGEE-2 project has collected extensive datasets from chemically rare stars in our galaxy and its satellite galaxies. While many of these stars reside in the galactic halo, there's a notable group of halo stars within the Milky Way that exhibit unusual chemical properties and have gone underutilized to date. A new analysis of residual abundances offers a new framework for analyzing these chemically distinctive stars and their stellar populations. By examining the patterns of abundance variations relative to iron, the study provides a enhanced understanding of the processes that formed the galaxy's central region and the halo, particularly the role of multiple nucleosynthetic sources and mass transfer between stars. These new results also provide the basis for a revised two-component halo model that better explains the distribution of elemental abundances within the galaxy. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a distinct population of extremely metal-poor stars associated with the galactic bulge, with chemical properties that bridge the gap between the galaxy's central region and the halo, and suggest that the galaxy's central region and the halo formed simultaneously, with no significant time lag. The study's findings are supported by theoretical models of gas-rich galaxy mergers and provide a foundation for future research aimed at further exploring the galaxy's central region and the halo using more precise abundance measurements. The analysis of residual abundances also offers a valuable tool with applications to future spectroscopic surveys, with the potential to shed light on the formation and evolution of satellite galaxies like the Milky Way. The current study is primarily based on data from 7,413 chemically rare stars in the APOGEE-2 dataset, including stars in the galactic halo with [Fe/H] less than -1.5 and chemical abundances that exhibit unusual patterns when compared to their peers. The research provides a framework for analyzing chemically distinctive stars and their stellar populations that can be used in future surveys of the galactic bulge, satellite galaxies, and the halo of the Milky Way. The study's findings have implications for our understanding of the galaxy's formation and evolution, particularly the role of mass transfer between stars and the availability of heavy elements for star formation in the halo. The analysis of residual abundances also reveals the limitations of current stellar evolution models, particularly their inability to fully explain the distribution of elemental abundances within the galaxy, particularly for stars with masses between 0.8 and 1.1 solar masses. The study suggests that future research should prioritize more precise abundance measurements of the galaxy's central region and the halo using higher signal-to-noise ratio

By developing a suitable expansion for the free energy around the universal critical point, we have derived explicit expressions for magnetic susceptibility in both 2 and 3 dimensions. Notably, in 2 dimensions near the nematic critical point, the magnetic susceptibility exhibits a distinctive cusp-like behavior, whereas in 3 dimensions it displays a more general universal $\chi$-shaped appearance under varying external stress. As for the real part of the magnetic susceptibility in 2 dimensions, it can be approximated as an expansion of a specific function, while in 3 dimensions it follows a more intricate pattern influenced by both real and imaginary components of the order parameter. Our research also highlights the significance of proper treatment of the imaginary component of the order parameter in evaluating magnetic susceptibility, as well as the necessity of expanding the free energy in a manner that accurately accounts for the topological features of the Fermi surface. If-then relation extraction is a significant component of commonsense knowledge, and many current approaches rely on deep neural networks. Despite these networks' effectiveness, they often struggle with if-then statements that involve implicit connections. To address this challenge, we investigate the utility of training neural networks on the hierarchical structure of if-then relation types. Our research introduces a novel framework that categorizes if-then relations into several types, including cause--effect, condition--sufficiency, equality, inclusion, and contrast. We then create a large-scale dataset consisting of 15,500 if-then statements with corresponding relation labels and part-of-speech tags. Quantum computers promise substantial performance improvements for certain linear algebra tasks, particularly matrix inversions, which underlie numerous high-stakes simulations like quantum chemistry applications. Despite the potential, current quantum devices are plagued by errors and cannot efficiently solve complex problems. A modified HHL algorithm, tailored for these near-optimal quantum machines, aims to minimize quantum computations while maximizing classical preprocessing. We've developed a novel variant of the HHL algorithm, NISQ-HHL, which minimizes the number of qubits required and reduces computation time by incorporating classical matrix decomposition. Our solution also includes a novel method for approximating matrix entries using qubit-based interpolation. When executed on a qubit device, NISQ-HHL showcases a 6.3 times reduction in computation time and a 3.9 times decrease in qubit usage when applied to a representative chemistry simulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Quantum-Art/NISQ-HHL. We've further developed a framework, QChemSim, which employs NISQ-HHL to efficiently simulate molecular properties, already demonstrating a 10-fold speedup over a classical simulator for a representative chemistry simulation on 7 qubits. This speedup can be achieved on existing quantum devices with real hardware, as seen in experiments using a 7-qubit Rydberg device. We anticipate a more significant impact on more complex applications in the future. Our research is accessible at https://qchemsim.org/. Our team is open to collaborations with other research groups and device manufacturers with regards to further optimizing NISQ-HHL for various quantum hardware platforms. Our code is designed to be versatile and can be adapted for other linear algebra applications beyond QChemSim. Our team is also available for custom requests and is willing to modify the code to suit specific needs. Our research and code can be used as a starting point for developing a wide range of linear algebra algorithms tailored to various quantum hardware devices. We believe our solution, NISQ-HHL, represents a significant breakthrough in executing complex linear algebra tasks on quantum devices, as demonstrated by our experimental results on a 7-qubit device from the Quantum Classical Simulation Lab at the University of Technology Sydney. We are confident that our algorithm and associated framework will facilitate widespread adoption of quantum devices in various chemistry simulations, among other applications. Our bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM), which is an enhancement over conventional attention mechanisms, facilitates the exchange of vital details between the two streams of our deep neural network model. Specifically, BiAM enables the linguistic stream to highlight the most crucial elements of the speech representations, while the speech stream helps to clear up any ambiguities in the linguistic stream, thereby preventing overgeneration of outputs. We have applied BiAM to a state-of-the-art end-to-end speech recognition model in both the sequence-to-sequence and convolutional neural network architectures. Our results show a significant reduction in word error rates of 8.8% and 5.9% for the two models respectively, without any additional labeled data. Our proposed BiAM achieves these gains without any additional parameters, making it a highly effective and efficient technique for enhancing the performance of automated speech recognition systems. In addition to adjustable voltage thresholds, this dual-nanowire setup enhances data accuracy, eliminates errors caused by nanowire imperfections, and facilitates clear identification of the transition points. As a result, sensitive voltage meters utilizing these nanowire pairs can accurately measure very low voltages with high precision. This breakthrough paves the way for the development of precise voltage meters that can measure extremely small voltages with great accuracy, potentially exceeding the limits of current standards. This innovative technique's effectiveness is showcased in a demonstration of a voltage meter capable of accurately measuring the 1 $\mu$V quantum fluctuations inherent in a Josephson junction, surpassing the precision achievable with individual nanowires. This groundbreaking method has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of voltage meters based on superconducting nanowires, expanding their applications in the measurement of tiny voltages in quantum systems and in sensitive voltage metrology. We analyze how a combination of regularization and constraint techniques in neural network training can be informed by a focus on a network's Lipschitz character. We begin by establishing relationships between the $p$-norm of a neural network's weights and its Lipschitz constant, with the latter dependent on the $p$-norm for a specific choice of $p$. We then examine the impact of various optimization methods, including matrix norm regularization and constraint methods, on the $p$-norm of the network's weights. Our findings show that these methods are equivalent to minimizing the Lipschitz constant, providing a new interpretation of how they affect the network's predictions. Finally, we investigate how different $p$-norms influence the performance of these methods, with particular emphasis on how they constrain the network's capacity to map inputs, finding that they affect the network's ability to maintain a small Lipschitz constant and thereby preventing it from imposing unnecessary restrictions on the network's capacity. We conclude by exploring the scope for future work, including the examination of how different activation functions impact the network's Lipschitz character and the development of optimization algorithms that directly target the Lipschitz constant. This note describes the NLO+PS signal simulation method for vector leptoquark searches at the LHC, where NLO+PS stands for Next-to-Leading Order Partonic. To enhance the effectiveness of signal simulations, we have developed a vector leptoquark NLO generator using the Sherpa framework, in conjunction with the MadGraph import utility. By leveraging the MadGraph import utility, we have created a vector leptoquark model database for MadGraph, which enables the generation of NLO cross-sections for various partonic processes involving leptoquarks. In the NLO+PS approach, NLO cross-section calculations are combined with MultiPartonicInteraction, a tool for simulating hadron collisions at the Leading Order level. This methodology enhances signal modeling by incorporating NLO corrections to the cross-section, in addition to the effects of parton showers and hadronization. As a result, NLO+PS signal simulations provide a more precise model of final-state particles, in comparison to LO simulations. In the context of vector leptoquark searches, this precision is particularly valuable for modeling the semileptonic decay process $l \nu b \bar{l}$, where the main background is dominated by leptons from the decay of hadrons. To validate the NLO+PS approach, we have conducted a series of comparisons involving different leptoquark masses, energies, and particle types, in addition to an assessment of the method's performance for modeling the background. Furthermore, we have established an upper limit on the cross-section for NLO+PS signal simulations in the $m\mathrm{LQ} > 350$ GeV range, in accordance with the search strategy employed in recent LHC experiments. In order to facilitate seamless integration with existing search codes, we have developed an interface for importing NLO+PS signal events into Delphes, a fast simulation toolkit. In order to facilitate the generation of NLO+PS cross-sections for partonic processes involving leptoquarks, we have created a vector leptoquark model database for MadGraph, which enables the efficient creation of these cross-sections. In order to expedite the development of NLO generators for Sherpa, we have also developed a vector leptoquark NLO generator for this purpose. In order to facilitate the comparison of NLO+PS predictions with experimental data, we have conducted an assessment of the method's performance for modeling the background in semileptonic searches for vector leptoquarks.

To reduce radiation exposure during PET scans, a deep-neural-network (DNN)-based framework is proposed to generate high-dose PET images from low-dose ones with the assistance of PET-MRI data. In order to improve image quality, the technique uses two DNN models to train images: one focused on directly producing high-quality PET images and the other aimed at creating both high- and low-dose PET images. Both models are trained to minimize the difference between actual and simulated PET-MRI data through two separate training processes, and the generated images are utilized in the first model to produce the final high-dose PET images. The technique was tested on 20 real patients who had undergone both PET and MRI scans, and it demonstrated the capability to reduce noise in PET images while preserving anatomical details. By comparing the technique with standard reconstruction methods, the proposed framework showed significant improvements in image quality metrics, particularly in assessing lesions in clinical settings. Additionally, the technique was found to be computationally efficient and capable of creating high-dose PET images from varying low-dose scan levels with little compromise in image quality. In order to facilitate clinical adoption, a functional code of the technique was created for use in research settings. All codes are accessible on GitHub, and the technique is also being further developed as part of research ongoing at the corresponding author's institution. This study investigates how contextualized word embeddings influence the performance of neural coreference systems when applying centering theory. Unlike previous work, our research compares the performance of multiple neural coreference frameworks using both standard coreference metrics and theoretical measures derived from centering theory, with the aim of examining the impact of contextualized embeddings within these frameworks. Our experiments indicate that contextualized embeddings improve the coreference system's performance and its consistency with centering theory. We also found that the system's adherence to centering theory predicts its performance on certain coreference metrics. Furthermore, our research reveals that the system's adherence to centering theory is influenced by its ability to identify and link nominal expressions, but is not significantly impacted by the system's ability to identify and link pronouns. In addition, we found that the system's adherence to centering theory is affected by the text being processed, but not by the level of training data. Our findings provide a deeper understanding of the relationships between neural coreference systems, centering theory, and contextualized word embeddings, with implications for future research and development in these areas. By analyzing various filling patterns and their dynamics, we find that many patterns result in a threshold current that is lower than the optimal value, and only specific patterns can achieve the optimal balance. By utilizing this method, we find that an appropriate filling pattern can significantly enhance the versatility of energy-recovery linacs, allowing for a current margin of at least two times greater than previously possible. Additionally, this approach allows for the development of a design tool that can be utilized to create efficient and robust energy-recovery linacs by selecting the optimal filling pattern in conjunction with other design parameters, such as cavity geometry and beam energy. This involves integrating a six-gluon amplitude from $ \mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, where all external particles except one have zero helicity. This allows for a comparison of the two approaches, confirming the equivalence of their underlying physics. Furthermore, a connection between the two approaches becomes apparent through the insertion of a specific field into a three-gluon vertex. A three-gluon vertex in QCD can also be completely reconstructed from the two-gluon CEV, providing a novel alternative to other methods. This represents a rare example of a three-gluon vertex that lacks any collinear or ultra-violet (UV) divergences, making it particularly unique. This achievement also highlights the two-gluon CEV as a fundamental and non-trivial object in its own right. This research demonstrates the capability to extend the analysis to higher-order vertices, offering a promising avenue for exploring vertices of any order. This is made possible by employing a recently developed recursive structure associated with the two-gluon CEV. This name is inspired by the partonic structure of the two-gluon CEV, which resembles a "glue" that combines two individual particles into a single vertex. The stretching free energy of a polymer brush is examined on a surface with varying curvature, represented as a mathematical surface in 3D space. To simplify the analysis, we consider flat and curved surfaces that can be smoothly transformed into each other. Mathematical techniques are employed to minimize the free energy change when the surface curvature changes, while maintaining the fixed end-to-end distance of the polymer chain. The resulting expression for free energy change is expressed in terms of a gamma function, depending on the surface curvature and the fixed end-to-end distance of the polymer chain. The impact of surface curvature on free energy change is also compared with existing models, which assume either small or large curvatures. The analysis can be applied to a variety of surfaces, including those with non-zero Gaussian curvature in three-dimensional space, as well as surfaces with constant positive or zero curvature in two-dimensional space. The effects of surface tension and solvation energy on the free energy change are also discussed, including their impact on polymer brush thickness. The study provides an expression for the average end-to-end distance of the polymer chain in a brush, which is influenced by surface curvature, surface tension, solvation energy, and the fixed end-to-end distance. The resulting expressions can be applied to polymer brushes situated on the surface of solid particles, in nanocapillaries, or within vesicles. The analysis provides a framework for understanding and predicting the behavior of polymer brushes situated on surfaces with constant positive or zero curvature in two-dimensional space, as well as surfaces with non-zero Gaussian curvature in three-dimensional space. The study highlights the limitations of existing models, which cannot accurately describe the behavior of polymer brushes situated on the surface of solid particles, in nanocapillaries, or within vesicles. We develop a method to model peer effects as variations in individual outcomes based on their connections to others in the network, taking into account the complex structures and diverse relationships within it. The approach involves using geometric interpretations to derive efficient estimation procedures for peer effects and network effects in equations that are nonlinear and endogenous. We demonstrate the validity and performance of our approach through Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we apply this method to an empirical analysis of how college roommates' academic performance influence each other, taking into account the varying sizes and types of the connections between individuals in the network. The results show that there are significant peer effects within these networks of connections. Deeper analysis of protein folding pathways is possible through the use of advanced simulations and techniques such as molecular dynamics and protein folding algorithms. Recent advancements have been made in this area, but there's still a significant lack of data regarding the intermediate structures that form during the folding process. A new method has been developed to track the intricate details of protein folding, including the formation of knots within polypeptide chains. This approach, which utilizes advanced graph theory to analyze simulation data, has been applied to the study of two specific protein structures known as protein A (or Trpzip) and protein GKN. Both of these proteins exhibit complex, shallow knot formations; however, their folding pathways differ significantly. While deeply knotted proteins tend to follow similar folding patterns as their non-knotted counterparts, the data suggests that the folding pathways of shallow knotted proteins are more fragmented and less predictable. Furthermore, research indicates that the formation of knots within protein structures occurs randomly, rather than being an integral part of their folding process, as hypothesized previously. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the importance of thoroughly examining intermediate structures and folding pathways in order to fully comprehend the complex mechanisms underlying protein folding, and the need for more efficient protein folding algorithms that allow for the detailed tracking of secondary structure formation and knotted structures. DeepSeeding Counterfactuals Online (DISCO) is a novel approach that utilizes
counterfactual data generation for machine learning robustness and generalization.
During training, counterfactual data with the opposite label is created, and
models are taught to distinguish between genuine and fabricated samples. Developed
primarily for classification tasks, DISCO demonstrates its potential for
adversarial resistance and improved performance when combining primary and
counterfactual datasets. Our research expands upon DISCO by integrating counterfactual data
into the regression classification task known as A/B testing, a fundamental
problem in its own right. We refer to this method as DeepSeeding Counterfactuals
for A/B Testing, or DCABT. When counterfactual data is incorporated, DCABT
takes the form of a multi-task learning problem. We test the efficacy of DCABT
under various conditions, including both linear and logistic models, with
counterfactual data generated via REINFORCE and the ADjoint framework. Our
results indicate that incorporating counterfactual data boosts the accuracy of
A/B testing models, with the added bonus of withstanding both adversarial and
shift robustness testing. Our research demonstrates the versatility of DISCO
and the difficulties associated with evaluating methods that generate counterfactual
data. We open-source DCABT on GitHub, along with a companion notebook that
facilitates easy reproduction of our experiment for classification tasks. We
encourage further development of the framework by the machine learning community. We also provide a detailed guide for industry practitioners looking to apply DCABT to A/B testing regression classification tasks. We highlight potential areas of application, including recommendation systems, targeted advertising, and product placement. We propose a method for determining the ideal amount of counterfactual data necessary for industry practitioners, while industry practitioners with large amounts of data can simply incorporate counterfactuals into their existing testing workflows. We outline the steps for replicating our research, which involves conducting A/B testing with a wide range of subjects, including university students, Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, and industry employees, as well as conducting robustness and shift testing with real-world data sets, including both linear and logistic models. We make the necessary code and data sets available online. We conclude by highlighting the limitations of our research, including the difficulty of defining counterfactuals, the risk of overfitting, the difficulty of evaluating methods that generate counterfactuals, and the need for more diverse and complex datasets. Human annotators typically assign one or several labels to a piece of text during the labeling process. Unfortunately, the true label distribution is often unknown and cannot be utilized during training, as deep learning models require a fixed number of labels per sample. To address this challenge, a new sampling method called single-to-multi (S2M) is proposed to generate high-quality multi-label data with minimal annotation costs. By taking a single labeled instance and determining the relevant labels based on a similarity threshold, the model is able to assign labels to new, unlabeled texts. By combining S2M with a state-of-the-art neural free text generation model, our approach achieves both quantitative and qualitative improvements over standard supervised and unsupervised generation tasks. Our method also offers significant cost savings, as it requires only 10 labeled instances per new data set, compared to 10,000 unlabeled instances required for unsupervised generation. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/zhongjieLASDGUO/S2M-LF.

These concepts can be applied to mediating monads via adjunctions, providing a framework that extends the theory of adjunctions for monads. We explore the relationship between weak naturality and the weakened universal properties, establishing conditions under which they coincide. Furthermore, we investigate the implications for controlled intermediate layers and strong/weak adjoint monad pairs within this framework. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that weak naturality and the associated universal property serve as a minimum common denominator for the theories of strong and weak adjunctions for monads. We also discuss the connections to Beck's monadicity theorem and the theories developed by Seely, Moggi, and Curry-Howard. The high sensitivity of point process methods such as Hawkes processes makes them ideal for detecting patterns in noisy data, particularly those representing sudden events like heartbeats. Although these methods effectively identify cardiac arrhythmias in clean data, they struggle with noisy data, leading to incorrect conclusions about underlying cardiac dynamics. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach that combines point process methods with a Gaussian white noise filter, resulting in the Noisy SPATIAL Noisy HP model. We prove the existence and uniqueness of a solution to this model and derive an estimator for its parameters. Through simulations, we demonstrate that this model detects cardiac arrhythmias more accurately than the original Hawkes process approach in noisy data settings. Furthermore, we apply this model to an empirical example involving heart rate data from a healthy individual during exercise, and the results reveal that it effectively identifies dynamic changes in the cardiac dynamics even in the presence of significant noise. This model's effectiveness is further validated by a comparison with the original Hawkes process through statistical tests. We also investigate the model's performance across varying noise levels and data lengths. This study presents FedHealth, a novel federated learning framework designed for wearable activity recognition models. Due to the privacy concerns of users, medical data cannot be shared freely, thus preventing the sharing of raw data during a federated learning process. As a result, research on wearable activity recognition using federated learning is impeded. To address this challenge, FedHealth proposes an innovative approach that enables the dissemination of transformed data instead of raw data. To facilitate secure data sharing, a specialized protocol has been developed, enabling users to transmit feature vectors instead of raw data. Furthermore, FedHealth includes an innovative protocol for secure data aggregation, allowing users to transmit feature vectors instead of raw data. By doing so, users can maintain their privacy while sharing data. By conducting experiments on real-world datasets, the study demonstrates its effectiveness. In particular, FedHealth significantly enhances the accuracy of wearable activity recognition by 11% and 15% in comparison with centralized learning and traditional federated learning, respectively. Additionally, the study highlights the significance of model updating, data retainer, and hyperparameter tuning in wearable activity recognition using federated learning. In particular, FedHealth achieves the highest accuracy when models are frequently updated, data retainer is used, and hyperparameters are properly set, resulting in accuracy rates of 43.6%, 51.8%, and 55.1% respectively. Portfolio management strategies aim to achieve optimal performance based on various criteria and constraints, with different optimization approaches leading to various methods such as utility and multi-objective optimization, Bayesian learning, and machine learning. This paper classifies optimization approaches and methods for portfolio performance based on utility, risk-parity, and data-driven frameworks, examining the trade-offs between predicted performance and risk, as well as the suitability for applications in different markets and scenarios. Furthermore, the paper discusses future research directions, potential challenges, and new methods for portfolio performance optimization, including the utilization of machine learning methods, risk management models, and deep learning techniques. This comprehensive review provides a theoretical foundation for an ongoing project aimed at developing an autonomous portfolio management system using reinforcement learning. This system will be tested and compared with other methods using simulated data, with plans for future application to a real-world portfolio based on the Nikkei 225 index. System evaluation metrics are proposed, including the application of portfolio performance metrics such as Sharpe ratio and Treynor ratio. This paper is an extension of previous research on utility-based portfolio optimization and risk management models, with additional discussion on machine learning methods and metric evaluation to ensure clarity for readers without a technical background in mathematics and computer science. This research is part of an ongoing project that also includes research on a real-world application to the Nikkei 225 index with results compared to well-known portfolio management methods such as MVO and RB. The recruitment process, particularly for positions that require assessing applicants through interviews, can be quite time-consuming due to the sheer number of applicants. To streamline panel-based interviews with multiple assessors, the process can be divided into two stages: creating the panel schedule and assigning it to applicants. To tackle the scale of modern recruitment, developing algorithms is crucial to make this process manageable. This paper outlines two approaches to efficiently create panel schedules and board panels by minimizing the number of interviews and assessing the computational complexity of the algorithms. It also highlights the benefits and limitations of these methods and provides code for easy use and customization by others. To demonstrate the practical applications of these algorithms, the paper includes an in-depth case study of a real-world recruitment scenario. It is worth noting that the code and research presented in this paper can be applied to a broader context of scheduling interviews with multiple assessors, not limited to recruitment practices. This research focuses on the underlying goal of optimally choosing payoffs in a context influenced by a diffusion that adheres to a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE). As the underlying diffusion evolves, the optimal payoff may change, and we aim to determine the fair value of a derivative that is sensitive to this diffusion, even in the presence of multiple such diffusions, some of which may be correlated. We begin by analyzing a single diffusion and derive a formula for the optimal payoff, which takes the form of a gain process subject to a restriction, and subsequently determine its fair value as the sum of its current value and the present value of future expected costs. This process can be viewed as the solution to a modified BSDE with a drift component that is driven by the underlying stochastic process, a Brownian motion, and a source term that includes the payoff itself and the value of future payoffs, both of which are measurable with respect to the forward flow of information. We also consider a scenario with multiple diffusions and derive formulas for the optimal payoff and its fair value in this case. Finally, we conclude by examining the relationship between our results and existing literature on the subject, including notable connections to the Heston model of stochastic volatility. The significant rise of the lepton pair invariant mass at the Large Hadron Collider prompts an examination of the asymmetric production process for leptoquarks, a process that can result in distinctive signals via same-sign lepton final states. To achieve meaningful contributions from this process, leptoquarks must be heavy enough to avoid being too extensively constrained by other particle interactions, and their coupling must be quite strong to ensure they are readily detectable. In the context of the Standard Model and its most prevalent extensions, we investigate the asymmetric production process for leptoquarks and identify the relevant experimental data. Furthermore, we discuss how recent findings from the 7 and 8 TeV LHC datasets constrain the parameters of several popular theories that incorporate leptoquarks. In addition, we outline potential discovery channels and estimate the capabilities of the 13 TeV LHC to shed light on existing knowledge and to guide ongoing and future experimental efforts. In doing so, we outline the possibilities for the direct detection of leptoquarks at the LHC and other suitable particle accelerators. Additionally, we examine the prospects for detecting leptoquarks that decay into neutral Higgs bosons and that could give rise to a 125 GeV Higgs state within the Standard Model or its most widely accepted extensions. In these scenarios, we consider both conventional and exotic Higgs decay channels to provide a comprehensive understanding of the challenges and opportunities at hand. In the process, we establish the maximum mass range that a leptoquark can have while being compatible with recent experimental constraints from the LHC, especially in the context of the most commonly examined leptoquark models that incorporate scalar and vector leptoquarks. In these models, we explore the potential for the 125 GeV Higgs state to be composed of both heavy and light leptoquark components, or solely of heavy leptoquarks, with mass ranges that could extend beyond 500 GeV. To achieve this, we examine current limits on leptoquark masses and explore the potential for the 7, 8, and 13 TeV LHC to give rise to a 125 GeV Higgs state that could result from the decay of leptoquarks, with mass ranges that could significantly exceed the current limits of the LHC. In doing so, we outline the discovery channels for the 125 GeV Higgs state at the 13 TeV LHC and the requirements for its direct detection. We employed MEGARA to analyze the spatially-resolved, ground-based spectra of a highly luminous, extremely metal-poor galaxy at 1.4 Gyrs distance, containing intense emission lines resulting from Charge-Exchange (CI) and the presence of circumgalactic gas. The spectra were mapped across the galaxy's extent of approximately 24kpc, allowing us to investigate the distribution of CI line ratios that could indicate the presence of low-density gas within the galaxy's wind or its surrounding environment. By comparing these ratios to those produced through photoionization, we found a possible connection between the highest CI line ratios and the galaxy's central region. However, the majority of the spectra could be explained by a combination of the galaxy's stellar population, stellar winds, and ongoing star formation, combined with the dispersion of line ratios indicative of the galaxy's overall abundance that resists the influence of local environments. Ultimately, the spectra provided no clear evidence for the presence of gas within the galaxy's wind or its surrounding environment, offering valuable constraints on its possible composition and distribution. Additionally, the galaxy's overall CI line ratios align with those observed in galaxy clusters at similar redshifts, suggesting that extreme starburst galaxies at this stage may be surrounded by similar gas reservoirs. Furthermore, the analysis of the galaxy's abundance through CI line ratios was found to be more reliable than other methods, given its resistance to the dispersion of line ratios and the metallicity of the galaxy itself. Consequently, we propose the use of CI line ratios as a valuable tool in the study of the abundance of galaxies at this stage of evolution. Lastly, we emphasize the potential of ground-based, spatially-resolved spectra in the study of galaxies at 1 Gyrs distance through the use of advanced spectrographs like MEGARA.

We investigate the ASEP's dynamics from a new perspective by examining the kinetic seeds model, where particles of two distinct classes compete for step opportunities. Our study focuses on the motion of second-class particles and demonstrates that their average velocity varies over time before eventually reaching a steady-state limit. As time progresses, the velocity of these particles can be represented through a gamma function, whose parameters evolve in a manner influenced by the initial conditions. Although the limiting velocity is uniformly 1/2 for all second-class particles, the initial time period in which the shift occurs differs for each particle, directly correlating with its initial distance from the origin. Furthermore, we observe that the resulting velocity distribution exhibits ASEP-specific characteristics, displaying a distinct pattern before reaching its final, uniform form. Our research also reveals the integrated velocity distribution evolves into a time-dependent form of the gamma distribution, ultimately transforming into an equilibrium state represented by the Bernoulli distribution. We support our findings by presenting numerical data obtained from simulations of the ASEP. As the kinetic seeds model can be considered a variant of the TASEP with injection and removal points, our study's results are applicable, providing new insights into the TASEP's dynamics. Epidemiological research relies on ordinary differential equation-based models to analyze and understand the spread and control of diseases. Although these mathematical models are effective at fitting available data, they may generate unrealistic trajectories outside the observed period, which could lead to biased inferences and limit the biological feasibility of the model. To address this challenge, we developed a new method for fitting differential models that prioritizes the coherence of the model's trajectory and adheres to the principle of biological plausibility. By redefining the model's parameters to focus on its dynamic behavior rather than the fit to past data, we ensure that the model's predictions for the future are reliable and align with observed patterns in the data. By considering the future as part of the present, we ensure that the model remains biologically feasible across all time periods. To achieve this, we employ a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm that simulates the model's parameter posterior distribution while ensuring that the model's trajectory complies with predefined conditions, which can be set to reflect specific constraints such as non-negativity of the model's variables or their monotonicity. By incorporating these constraints into the model, we can guarantee the biological feasibility of the model, even when the model itself is complex and nonlinear. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we applied it to a Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model, fitting it to real data from the 2019-2020 COVID-19 pandemic in Santa Clara County, California. Our results show that this method yields a coherent and biologically plausible model that accurately predicts the future spread of the disease and informs public health policy. Lately, research involving cold atoms has focused on a critical system that exhibits both pendulum-like behavior and non-rigidity, leading to atom-molecule conversion and the emergence of instabilities. A team of scientists has developed an efficient numerical method to simulate large-scale multi-dimensional lattices using a simplified effective model, and they have demonstrated how this model captures intricate dynamics, including pendulum-like motion, atom-molecule conversion, and the breakdown of stability, within the multi-dimensional lattices. By using this streamlined model to simulate a specific configuration, consisting of two coupled pendulum-like systems connected by a bridge, they have observed the complex interplay of multiple wave-like modes, the formation of atom-molecule patterns, and the eventual collapse into a stable molecule. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of the non-rigid pendulum model, providing valuable insights into the intricate dynamics of atom-molecule conversion and offering a versatile tool for exploring a wide range of related phenomena with diverse configurations. As DNA data storage continues to mature, managing storage partitions becomes increasingly important to facilitate efficient file retrieval. A key aspect of this management involves the process of PCR primer walking, where multiple overlapping DNA sequences are amplified using sets of primers that target specific file partitions. To streamline this process and minimize the number of polymerase chain reactions required, a high degree of overlap is desired between adjacent partitions. To achieve this efficiently, our proposed system utilizes a binary matrix to represent overlapping relationships between partitions, modelled as interval graphs, and employs a heuristic algorithm to determine the optimal order in which to amplify the partitions, aiming to minimize the number of reactions needed while adherating to desired overlap levels. Our system also includes a decoder that converts encoded DNA files into suitable partition formats, capable of reversing the amplification process through targeted resequencing. To validate our system's effectiveness, a mock DNA storage system was established, consisting of 102 encoded files totalling 62 Mbp of DNA, on which our system successfully retrieved all files with an average of 12.5 reactions per file, or approximately 500x coverage per reaction. To further illustrate the system's efficiency, a real-world application was explored, where a previously encoded collection of 500 research papers was accurately retrieved from a 38 Mbp DNA dataset, requiring approximately 500x coverage per reaction. Precise riverbed bathymetry estimation is crucial for accurately understanding and predicting river dynamics, especially during flooding events. Typically, bathymetry is determined through costly and complex measurements like acoustic or optical scanning, but these methods are often impractical for real-time, long-distance river monitoring. This paper presents a novel approach, the Principal Component Geostatistical Algorithm (PCGA), designed to efficiently determine bathymetry along an entire river segment using flow velocity measurements from surface floats as input. By treating bathymetry estimation as a geostatistical regression problem and leveraging the PCGA framework, this method effectively accounts for spatial correlations and river variability. The algorithm was tested on a 90 kilometer stretch of the Mississippi River near the confluence with the Ohio River, resulting in a 20% improvement in bathymetry estimation accuracy when compared to traditional geostatistical methods. Furthermore, PCGA demonstrated the ability to estimate bathymetry along an entire river segment, including the confluence areas, which pose significant estimation challenges. By incorporating flow velocity measurements from floats with varying depth sensors, PCGA was able to estimate depth with a median error of 0.19 meters or less within the entire river segment, except for the confluence areas with higher error rates. This novel approach offers a practical solution for monitoring rivers and their dynamics by combining flow velocity measurements with the PCGA algorithm. By applying the characteristic classes introduced by Guillermier to a specific combination of maps, the Madsen-Weiss theorem can be reinterpreted as a instance of the B-principle in the topological category. A persistent assumption in the analysis of stochastic processes is that random fluctuations can be accurately described by Gaussian diffusion models. However, actual data frequently exhibit correlations and heterogeneity that contravene this standard, thereby affecting the validity of these models. We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the following discrete stochastic process: it begins with a uniformly distributed initial state, undergoes periodic advection, and ends with spatially extended source/sink reactions that generate correlations and heterogeneity. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that this process displays surprisingly coherent behavior that can be accurately explained by a Gaussian diffusion model, despite the presence of correlations and heterogeneity. We have further discovered that this model effectively captures the advection time scale and the intensity of the source/sink reactions. What is more, we have demonstrated that over time, this process evolves from being uniformly distributed to being peaked at one end, with the peak's location moving towards the source and the width of the distribution increasing in a square root manner. Furthermore, we have observed that this process exhibits a form of self-similarity that allows us to scale its time series data, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of its dynamics. We have also tested its robustness in the face of varying advection time scales, source/sink intensity levels, and different initial state conditions. All in all, this process offers a valuable tool for validating model-based analysis strategies that are widely used in the study of other complex time series data. We have made the code for our simulations publicly available on a reputable code sharing platform. We believe that this process has significant applications in various fields such as climate science, biology, and economics. We propose that it be referred to as the Standard Stochastic Advection-Dispersion-Reaction (SSADR) process. We have high hopes that this process will contribute meaningfully to advancing our understanding of random processes and their ability to generate surprisingly coherent behavior from initially random and uniformly distributed states. We have further suggested that it be considered a vital component of more complex systems that exhibit behavior we have not yet fully understood. We propose that future research initiatives be established to better comprehend the long-term evolution of the SSADR process, especially in relation to its connection to the Kolmogorov-Petrovskii-Piskunov equation, as well as its potential applications in modeling real-world phenomena that behave in analogous ways. We investigate the interplay between self-phase and cross-phase modulation within Identical Counterpropagating Modes in a Loop Resonator. Through numerical simulations, we compare the outcomes of self-phase and cross-phase modulation occurring at the same rate under identical conditions. As a result, we find that cross-phase modulation exhibits an order of magnitude greater strength than self-phase modulation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that cross-phase modulation can be reframed in terms of self-phase modulation strength and the overlap between the two counterpropagating beams. Ultimately, this equivalence in dynamics permits us to interpret various nonlinear phenomena, including soliton formation and noise suppression, through the dominant cross-phase modulation effects. Moreover, we show that a loop resonator configuration can serve as a nonlinear intensity interferometer, fueled by the significantly greater strength of cross-phase modulation compared to self-phase modulation. This finding provides a suitable platform for nonlinear optical applications, such as nonlinear noise filtration and soliton generation, with potential for scaling to high powers. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of nonlinear dynamics in loop resonators and related counterpropagating configurations.
