We outline a proposed atomic interferometry experiment that could identify the smallest possible local magnetic field values, specifically those below 10fT per barm, within a magnetic field detection area of approximately 10^-4 gauss/cm^2. This detection capability, which surpasses current magnetometers by several orders of magnitude, can be achieved by utilizing the sensitive phase shift induced by the local magnetic field in atomic interferometry, coupled with optimized design parameters such as atomic beam collimation, atomic species choice, and measurement duration. A proposed experiment featuring strontium atoms and a designed magnetic field gradient as the benchmark demonstrates the feasibility of this detection sensitivity. Furthermore, this experiment could also provide extremely low sensitivity measurements for magnetic fields in underground locations, as well as detecting transient magnetic field fluctuations. It is worth noting that the minimum detectable local magnetic field in this experiment can be further reduced by increasing the measurement time. A similar experiment with optimized design parameters could also serve as a highly sensitive magnetometer for static magnetic field detection in laboratory settings. A detection capability for static magnetic field gradients as low as 10^-4 gauss/cm^2, or equivalently a local magnetic field of around 10fT per barm, in underground locations or in a controlled laboratory environment, could serve as a benchmark for future atomic magnetometers employing similar design principles. A future experiment incorporating optically pumped spin-polarized atoms, in addition to achieving the aforementioned detection sensitivity for static magnetic fields, could also serve as a highly sensitive detector for transient magnetic field fluctuations, with detection capabilities for a wide range of applications including, but not limited to, geophysical research, archaeological site detection, and the study of magnetic fields in quantum mechanics and electromagnetism. We explore a Bayesian nonparametric framework for deconvolution where a Dirichlet process prior is applied to densities and another Dirichlet process prior is applied to the admixture weights. Under certain conditions, we demonstrate the unique identification of weights and show that they can be recovered using a stick-breaking representation. Additionally, we establish the asymptotic normality of the estimated weights. Furthermore, we provide a functional central limit theorem for the weighted average of densities. This is coupled with an application to identifying and estimating densities from admixture distributions in the context of population genetics. If the support of the admixture weights is finite, we propose an algorithm based on the method of moments to estimate these weights and the corresponding weighted average of densities. This algorithm is demonstrated to converge asymptotically, accompanied by an investigation into the asymptotic behavior of the estimated weights and the corresponding weighted average of densities. This is illustrated through simulations and an empirical example. This research is an extension of recent work by Berger and Yang (2017), (arXiv:1703.02752), (arXiv:1703.02757), and (arXiv:1703.02758). This research has also been inspired by the earlier findings of Auer, Segal, and Telgarsky (2015), (arXiv:1511.03769), and Diaconis and Freedman (1987), (arXiv:151100697). As artificial intelligence workloads continue to dominate high-performance computing with single GPUs, the traditional GPU memory allocator falls behind due to DynamiC memory management. DynaSOAr, a novel, two-level memory allocator is proposed to address this challenge. It divides memory into large blocks to facilitate fast, dynamic allocation within them. The results show that DynaSOAr achieves a 24.6x speedup and a 1.4x performance improvement compared to the current NVIDIA GPU memory allocator. It also outperforms the state-of-the-art, hand-tuned memory allocator, Cumulus, in terms of performance and memory usage. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's scalability is demonstrated by reducing the overall system memory usage by 21.6% when using four NVIDIA A100 GPUs. It also delivers a 10.4x speedup and a 1.2x performance boost when utilizing four A100 GPUs in a system. DynaSOAr is an open-source, publicly available memory allocator that can be used with various deep learning frameworks, including PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Cumulus. It is compatible with a wide range of NVIDIA GPUs, including the A100, H100, SXM2, and MIG memory configurations. System administrators can easily integrate DynaSOAr into their existing deep learning workflows by simply replacing the current memory allocator with DynaSOAr. It is worth noting that the development of DynaSOAr was carried out using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS with CUDA 11.3 and cuMemCheck 11.3. It is also important to note that DynaSOAr does not require any modifications to existing code or deep learning frameworks. It simply optimizes memory management for maximum performance and efficiency. It is anticipated that DynaSOAr will continue to improve memory management and performance in future NVIDIA GPU generations. In the future, possible enhancements to DynaSOAr could be explored, such as the integration of memory reclamation techniques like atomic instructions and lock-free memory allocators to further minimize memory fragmentation and improve overall performance. Additionally, future work could be dedicated to developing similar memory allocators for multi-GPU systems equipped with NVLink or InfiniBand interconnects. This could potentially lead to the development of more advanced memory allocators that leverage interconnect topology for enhanced memory management and performance. It is also possible to extend DynaSOAr for use in heterogeneous computing systems that combine CPUs and GPUs. The K2 mission from NASA has allowed the detection of countless planets that orbit stars similar to our own, and a recent study found that a significant portion of these planets could potentially support life. A new analysis reveals that planets like K2-18b, and possibly K2-22b, and K2-242b that reside within the "habitable zones" of their stars may not necessarily have conditions suitable for life as we know it. By examining the way these planets interact with their stars during transit, researchers found that mini-Neptunes like K2-18b likely have thick atmospheres that could prevent any potential surface from supporting life. Similarly, a study of K2-22b and K2-242b suggests that these planets also possess extensive gas layers that could make their surfaces uninhabitable. Although future observations from missions like the James Webb Space Telescope could provide more insight into the composition and environments of these planets, it's possible that many of the transiting worlds previously considered capable of supporting life may actually be less suitable than initially thought. Despite this, the study of K2-18b and other similar planets has significant value, as it offers a unique opportunity to examine the formation and evolution of gas-rich planets that are no longer forming new planets in our solar system. Additionally, analyzing the atmospheres of K2-18b and other mini-Neptunes could provide a better understanding of how extensive gas layers form around planets and how they change over time. The research on K2-18b, a planet located about 111 light-years from Earth, also sheds light on the potential for life on a planet with conditions similar to those of Earth. The study's findings on K2-18b, a planet about one and a half times the size of Earth with a surface temperature that was once suitable for life, shows that it likely has a thick atmosphere that could make its surfaces uninhabitable and may have formed as a result of gravitational interactions with other planets in its star system. The same analysis applied to K2-22b and K2-242b reveals that these planets, which are about one and a half times the size of Earth with surface temperatures that could support life, also possess extensive gas layers that could make their surfaces less suitable for life as we know it. The study on K2-18b, a planet located about 111 light-years from Earth, offers a better understanding of the formation and evolution of gas-rich planets that are no longer forming new planets in our solar system

We used first-principles calculations based on the spin-polarized DFT method to investigate the substitutional and interstitial sites of carbon and nitrogen in TiO2 anatase by placing one atom at a time within the crystal lattice. Our study focused on comparing the structural, electronic, and chemical properties of TiO2 with an atom in a substitutional site versus an interstitial site. When an atom occupies an interstitial site instead of substituting a Ti or O atom, it occupies a non-symmetrical location within the unit cell, resulting in distinct distribution of its multi-electron charge and chemical reactivity, particularly in relation to surface Ti atoms. These sites exhibit higher reactivity than the substitutional sites, which show more significant bonding with oxygen atoms and lesser availability of their multi-electron charge. Consequently, these interstitial sites are more prone to forming bonds with oxygen and hydroxyl groups in the presence of water, and less likely to act as charge carriers in photocatalytic reactions. Our predictions are consistent with experimental findings of surface defects in TiO2 anatase, particularly those altered by water, and suggest that surface Ti atoms play a crucial role in accommodating interstitial atoms. Our results also highlight the significance of accurately identifying the locations of surface defects in TiO2 anatase in order to comprehend their chemical properties. Our predicted energy levels of impurity levels in TiO2 anatase with interstitial atoms are comparable to those obtained through other theoretical methods, demonstrating the reliability of our first-principles calculations. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of carbon and nitrogen in TiO2 anatase with both substitutional and interstitial sites, and offers valuable insights into their chemical properties and reactivity. Our predicted energy levels of impurity levels in TiO2 anatase with interstitial atoms are comparable to those obtained through other theoretical methods, demonstrating the reliability of our first-principles calculations. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of carbon and nitrogen in TiO2 anatase with both substitutional and interstitial sites, and offers valuable insights into their chemical properties and reactivity. Our study is relevant to the photocatalytic activity of TiO2 anatase and suggests that surface defects with interstitial sites are less likely to act as charge carriers in photocatalytic reactions. Our study is also relevant to the biocidal properties of TiO2 anatase and implies that surface defects with interstitial sites are more prone to forming bonds with hydroxyl groups

Using semi-elastic process data from 35 pb^-1 of deep inelastic e^+p scattering at a center-of-mass energy of 318 GeV, the branching ratios for flavor changing neutral current decays of the top quark were examined and the following limits were established: B(t$\rightarrow$c$\gamma$) < 1.5 x 10^-4, B(t$\rightarrow$cZ) < 1.8 x 10^-4, B(t$\rightarrow$uZ) < 3.8 x 10^-4, and B(t$\rightarrow$u$\gamma$) < 0.9 x 10^-4 at the 95% confidence level. These limits are among the most stringent to date. The analysis employed the LHCb detector's zero-suppression and relied on estimates of non-perturbative corrections. The branching ratio limits were derived under assumptions of the effective Lagrangian approach to flavor changing neutral current interactions. The effective Lagrangian approach was found to be insufficient to describe the decay t$\rightarrow$uZ. The search was also expressed in terms of couplings to a generic massive neutral scalar, resulting in limits of O(10^-5) on B(t$\rightarrow$X) with no restriction on the final state. The results of the analysis await verification due to concerns about non-perturbative corrections and the need for further study of effective theories beyond the Lagrangian approach. The research indicates that deep inelastic scattering data can be a valuable source of constraints for certain effective theories. The most stringent limits derived in the analysis could be improved upon with access to a top quark or a generic massive neutral scalar with a mass below 7 GeV. The search for t$\rightarrow$u$\gamma$ or t$\rightarrow$c$\gamma$ in top quark production in proton-proton collisions at the LHC with the ATLAS and CMS detectors may offer the potential to further narrow the branching ratio limits by a factor of two or more. The current restriction on the effective coupling of a generic massive neutral scalar to the top quark could be replaced with a more precise effective theory or a specific model prediction. The research described in this paper remains the only example of a search for semi-elastic flavor changing neutral current decays of the top quark to date. The methods employed in the analysis have been largely automated and could be valuable for other exotic processes in semi-elastic channels. This edge-coloring problem has been examined on various types of graphs, including trees, with an aim to reduce the number of required colors. We have derived new lower bounds for the number of colors needed to color a specific shape of graphs, specifically a triangle, with distance $k$, denoted as $\chi_{d=k}(F)$. For a triangle, we proved that the minimum number of colors needed is $\lceil\frac{k}{2}\rceil+3$ when the distance between similarly colored edges is $k$, and this was further confirmed to be true for any tree when $k$ is $4$ or more. However, for $k$ less than $4$, we have no clear picture and it's unclear whether the lower bound of $3+k$ holds true. We have shown that the lower bound of $2+k$ holds true for the case of a triangle with $k$ equal to $2$ or $3$. In our analysis, we consider both Pauli and Haar randomised error scenarios. For both cases, we developed a qutrit measurement detection method that allows for the precise calculation of a system's tolerance to noise. Our approach also enables the computation of a parameter that indicates the number of qutrits that could be accurately determined as non-entangled within a given probability threshold. Furthermore, we compared the noise tolerance of qutrits and qubits under both Pauli and Haar randomised error scenarios with similar entropy levels. Our findings demonstrate that qutrits possess significantly greater tolerance to both bit-flip and arbitrary errors than qubits of equivalent complexity. Additionally, we established a lower and upper bound for the noise tolerance parameter $s$ in both the Haar and Pauli settings. Our research demonstrates the noise tolerance of qutrits to be directly proportional to their Hilbert space dimension, and we believe this characteristic presents a compelling reason for the potential use of qutrits in noisy measurement environments. In such settings, our findings suggest that qutrits could serve as more reliable determinations of a measured state than qubits of equivalent computational complexity. To meet the PANDA's sensitivity requirements, the PandaPrime experiment plans to highly polarize positrons through rare photon interactions using a magnetic spectrometer equipped with a imaging air Cherenkov (shiisho) detector and a radial neutron detector.  To evaluate the effectiveness of the polarization detection method, simulations of rare positron production were conducted.  By utilizing a machine learning algorithm to differentiate rare positron events from normal ones based on Cherenkov images, positron polarization degrees of 30% or greater can be identified with confidence levels of 99% or higher.  Additionally, the simulation demonstrates that the current PandaPrime design can achieve the desired polarization degree required for the PANDA experiment.  To further verify the effectiveness of the polarization detection method, a simulation of a specific rare reaction, namely rare electroweak charmonium decay into $\eta_c$, which involves highly polarized positrons, was conducted.  This simulation demonstrates that the PandaPrime experiment can detect $\eta_c$ via this rare process with an expected rate of approximately 12 events per year with background levels of less than 0.1 events per year.  Consequently, the PandaPrime experiment at the PANDA facility will have the capability to detect rare charmonium decay via rare electroweak processes with faithfulness to theoretical predictions.  Moreover, the experiment can also serve as a pioneering facility for detecting rare positron production at other future particle colliders, such as the ILC and CLIC. We introduce the notion of a topological groupoid extension, which serves as a topological counterpart to the concept of groupoid extensions in category theory. Topological groupoid extensions are then used to create a topological stack from a given site, mirroring the theoretical framework established by Moerdijk and Prestel for the topological realm. This leads to the discovery of a direct connection between topological groupoid extensions and topological gerbes constructed over specific topological stacks. Additionally, we demonstrate that there is a one-to-one correspondence between these gerbes and a particular subclass of topological etale stacks, which share similarities with Deligne's approach to defining gerbes within the algebraic setting. This connection also provides a natural link to the concept of gerbes within the topological context recently explored by Bénabes and Moerdijk. It's worth noting that our analysis can be seamlessly transferred to the realm of differential geometry by substituting the term "topological" with "smooth". Sincerely, Daniele Bartolini. A statistical analysis of molecular cores in the Perseus and Ophiuchi-II
clouds reveals the mass growth of cores over several million years and
provides insights into the formation of massive stars. Using submillimeter
cores identified in the Spitzer Polarimetry Target Survey, we tracked the
movement and mass evolution of these cores through repeated observations
over approximately 3 to 4 years with the Atacama kilometer Array. We then
selected cores that exhibited stable positions, showed no evidence of
disintegration, and had masses above 20 solar masses for further study. We
created sedimentation diagrams that illustrate the mass growth of these
cores, with some increasing in mass by 10 solar masses while others remain
stable or even decrease in mass. Although we cannot rule out the
disintegration of some cores, we propose that cores with masses above 60
solar masses are likely giving birth to massive stars. By examining the mass
growth of cores within 0.1 parsecs, we found that the mass growth rate per
million years is significantly higher for those that produce massive stars,
with an average mass increase of 20-60 solar masses compared to just 1
solar mass for others. This is consistent with the theory that massive stars
form from massive cores that quickly grow in mass over a relatively short
period, whereas intermediate-mass stars form from intermediate-mass cores
with a more gradual mass increase. We also observed that the mass growth
of cores is linked to the presence of massive protostars and young O-type
stars, and we propose a threshold mass of 60 solar masses for the formation
of massive stars that is supported by existing studies, although more
observations are needed to confirm this finding. We intend to repeat the
observations in the future to track the continued mass evolution of these
cores and shed more light on this subject. The data from this research is
available on the Atacama kilometer Array archive under the project code
2018.A.00021.S. The research also includes supplementary information that
can be accessed on the Spitzer Heritage Archive under the program ID 10081
and the project ID PTT. The research data and materials are governed by the
terms and conditions of their respective archives, and any reuse or
distribution of the data and materials must adhere to these guidelines. The
visual data used in the figures can be accessed on the Spitzer Science
Archive, the Atacama kilometer Array archive

This research examines how classical differentiation and integration impact the positivity of a type of function called a zonal function, which is highly symmetric and has beneficial properties. It's proven that standard differentiation and integration operators preserve the positivity of zonal functions. Additionally, a formula is provided for applying these operators to any given function, effectively serving as a mean-like operator when applied to a set of symmetric functions. The usefulness of these findings is demonstrated through applications to the preservation of positivity for specific types of functions, including polynomial-based zonal functions and Gaussian distributions in Euclidean spaces of various dimensions. The research also explores connections to classical results on the preservation of positivity by differentiation and integration operators, as well as the relationship to the Hamburger-Nevai theorem, which addresses the uniqueness of an arbitrarily defined moment sequence that satisfies specific conditions. The utility of these findings in reconstructing a function from its moments is highlighted, along with the implications for the uniqueness of these moment sequences. The research also delves into the characteristics of a type of zonal function called the radial Gaussian distribution, which serves as an infinite-dimensional example of a function with arbitrarily defined moments that can be shown to have a unique moment sequence, thus adhering to the principles outlined in the Hamburger-Nevai theorem. The relationship between the differentiation operator and the inverse of the moment operator is also explored, along with the properties of the operator that results from their composition. developing a roughness factor that simplifies their complex structure and
captures their mechanical properties. In this framework, we consider two main
 scenarios in which the flow of liquid foams can be analyzed: (1) the slow
drain of a single layer of foam and (2) the flow of multiple layers of foam.
For the slow drainage of a single layer of foam, we find that the relationship
between the surface tension, the viscosity of the liquid, and the roughness
factor is similar to that found by de Gennes et al., specifically $\tau \propto
\gamma R_{g}^{1/2}$, where $\tau$ is the shear stress, $\gamma$ is the
surface tension, $R_{g}$ is the roughness factor, and the gap time is given
by $\tau_{g} \propto \eta^{2} R_{g}^{2}$, where $\eta$ is the viscosity
of the liquid. For the flow of multiple layers of foam, we find that the
relationship between the pressure difference, the viscosity of the liquid, and
the roughness factor is given by $\Delta P \propto \eta^{2} R_{g}^{5}$, which
is consistent with experimental data collected from the drainage of layered
foams. Additionally, we find that the relationship between the shear stress and
the surface tension, the viscosity of the liquid, and the roughness factor is
given by $\tau \propto \gamma^{1/2} \eta^{1/2} R_{g}^{1/2}$, which is
also consistent with experimental data collected from the drainage of single
layers of foam. Notably, we find that the flow of layered foams can be
characterized by a single parameter, specifically the lambda ratio, which is
given by $\lambda = \frac{\eta^{2} R_{g}^{5}}{\Delta P}}$, which is
independent of the pressure difference and the viscosity of the liquid. We
also find that the flow of single layers of foam and layered foams can be
distinguished by the lambda ratio, which is given by $\lambda = \frac{\tau^{2}

Deep convolutional neural networks have achieved remarkable performance in various image classification tasks, yet ensemble-based convolutional neural networks have shown the ability to significantly boost their performance. This study explores the effectiveness of ensemble classifiers in relation to VGG16, a highly acclaimed network, and finds it can lead to a substantial increase in accuracy. We investigate multiple factors affecting the performance of these ensembles, including the selection of base classifiers, the method of combining their predictions, and the impact of overfitting. Additionally, a novel hybrid ensemble approach is proposed, which combines dropout regularization with an advanced voting technique to further enhance performance. This method demonstrates a significant gain in accuracy when applied to VGG16, with improvements of 12.2% and 10.6% in top1 and top5 accuracy in the CIFAR10 dataset and 10.4% and 5.5% in top1 and top5 accuracy in the CIFAR100 dataset, respectively. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of deep neural networks to achieve comparable or superior performance with minimal additional computational requirements. Code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuyu1998/Ensemble_VGG16.

When general relativity is combined with Chern-Simons theory in $2+1$ dimensions, a unique feature of rotating hairy black holes is observed - their entropy deviates from standard Chern-Simons predictions. Despite this anomaly, research indicates that this variation holds up across all angular momenta values. To further understand this phenomenon, an in-depth examination of the rotating hairy black holes' phase space is necessary. By re-expressing the model using a confinal mass variable, a surprising discovery is made - the dimensionless entropy of these black holes remains consistently one unit of entropy above the minimal allowed value, regardless of their mass or angular momentum. This finding provides a compelling explanation for the divergence from expected behavior. Additionally, by re-expressing the model using a rescaled mass variable, another variable becomes apparent that allows for the determination of the black hole's phase space based on just two variables - rather than the typical four. This reduced description reveals additional intriguing properties of these black holes, including the structure of their event horizons and the relationships between their mass, angular momentum, temperature, and entropy. Finally, an analysis of the conditions required for the formation of these black holes is presented, along with a discussion of the implications of their unique properties on the surrounding spacetime. This rotating solution provides a more accurate representation of the spacetime surrounding extremely fast rotating spinning top-like objects, particularly in the context of string theory. A key feature of this solution is the appearance of an inner boundary within the spinning top's own rotation axis, a phenomenon that has far-reaching implications for the study of spacetime structure caused by rotating, spinning objects. A critical challenge in elastography arises from the limited resolution of ultrasound imaging, particularly when determining axial and lateral tissue displacements from speckle patterns. A new nonlinear inversion algorithm is proposed to overcome this limitation by approximating the elastographic modulus based on the variance of axial displacements rather than the more difficult lateral displacements. Because pseudocodes can be either sequential or concurrent, with various logical specifications, a new, expressive formal framework is necessary to effectively examine their underlying characteristics. To achieve this, we developed an intricate framework comprising a diverse set of logical specifications, which allows us to create a method for comparing the behavioral similarities and differences between these specifications using an advanced form of graph theory known as the "reachability graph" (RG). We also created a more intricate version of RG, known as the "security reachability graph" (sRG), which serves as the basis for our novel security analysis, known as the "reachability-based interconnection" (rbi) method. By applying the rbi method to diverse sets of pseudocodes, we were able to uncover several critical issues, including the potential for data leaks, insecure password storage, and insecure use of cryptographic functions, among others. Furthermore, our research provides a set of guidelines for developing safe and secure pseudocodes, as well as a comprehensive evaluation of existing pseudocodes, including 17 well-known algorithms. In large-scale gridworlds with complex dynamics, efficient decision-making under uncertainty is crucial in high-stakes applications like security networking. A promising approach to streamline this process involves dividing the grid into distinct regions, or superstates, that represent meaningful environmental configurations. This study explores the benefits of such a state partitioning framework in a pursuit-evasion scenario where one agent seeks to evade another. A grid-resolving algorithm is introduced to create superstates that correspond to specific proximity relationships between the agents, and we analyze the computational costs and superstate partitioning strategies. Furthermore, an optimal decision-making policy is derived using a dynamic programming framework, and experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in efficiently navigating large gridworlds while evading capture. A key finding reveals that a fixed superstate partitioning size yields nearly optimal results across various grid sizes, except in very small gridsworlds. A notable observation from the experiments shows that the best policy strategies prioritize maintaining a safe distance from the pursuer rather than prioritizing evaporation, as might be expected. This study's contributions lie in its novel state partitioning algorithm, the grid-resolving algorithm, the benefits of superstates in decision-making under uncertainty in pursuit-evasion scenarios, and the insights gained from the experiments on the benefits of state partitioning in decision-making under uncertainty in pursuit-evasion scenarios. A superstate partitioning framework is also made available for download. A related question of interest in security networking involves an agent navigating a complex environment to locate a target node, and several algorithms exist for this task, including delta-star and grid-resolving, which are particularly effective in reducing computation costs in large-scale gridsworlds. However, neither of these algorithms generates a partitioned state space representation that could provide additional benefits for decision-making under uncertainty in pursuit-evasion scenarios. In contrast, the superstate partitioning framework offers a level of abstraction that could also be beneficial for target node search tasks, and it does so using a comparable computational cost to the delta-star algorithm. A key aspect of this study involves the development of a novel algorithm to partition the gridworld based on the proximity relationships between the agents, and this partitioning is referred to as a beta-state partitioning. A key observation from the experiments revealed that the best policy strategies for search and evasion scenarios often prioritize maintaining a safe distance from the pursuer rather than the target node, which could be an interesting insight for security networking applications. In 1936, Theodor Rosser significantly expanded Kurt Godel's first incompleteness theorem by
creating a formal system where any statement claiming its own undecidability within the
given framework is actually false. Additionally, Rosser demonstrated that for any given
formal system, there exists a statement expressing its own lack of provability within the
same framework, leading to his concept of "weak incompleteness." We will show that
this concept of weak incompleteness holds true for all formal systems that are capable
of capturing basic mathematical truths, or "primitive recursion." In doing so, we will
also establish the level at which these formal systems are capable of operating.
Furthermore, we will explore the relationship between Rosser's strengthening of Godel's
first incompleteness theorem and the concept of "Tarskian," which describes a
situation where a formal system is unable to demonstrate the inconsistency of a
subsystem comprising a subset of the original system's axioms. We will also
determine the maximum "Tarskian" level that a formal system can attain while still
incurring the consequences of weak incompleteness. We will achieve this by
introducing the concept of "extended arithmetical hierarchy," which serves as a
framework for examining the boundaries of formal systems that are capable of
capturing basic mathematical truths. We will also explore how this framework enables
us to identify the maximum level at which a formal system can operate while
incurring the consequences of both strong and weak incompleteness. We will
demonstrate that there are formal systems that can operate beyond the Scott
standard arithmetical hierarchy while still meeting the criteria of being
capable of capturing basic mathematical truths, or "primitive recursion." We will
also explore how these systems can be created through the addition of new axioms
while maintaining the level of "Tarskian" that they originally operated at. We
will establish that these added axioms will necessarily lead to the consequences
of both strong and weak incompleteness within these formal systems. We will
introduce a new arithmetical hierarchy, referred to as the "primary arithmetical
hierarchy," which serves as a framework for examining the boundaries of formal
systems that are capable of capturing basic mathematical truths, or "primitive
recursion," within the context of being capable of demonstrating the
inconsistency of a subsystem comprising a subset of the original system's axioms.

Researchers have observed the highest-resolution pulsar persistent scintles to date in PSR B1133+16, located approximately 1.77 kpc from Earth, by utilizing a combination of highly sensitive and stable radio telescopes at Westerbork. By analyzing the scintillation patterns over 24 years, they have mapped the distribution of individual scattering screens within the line of sight to the pulsar, discovering 15 distinct screens on average and gaining insight into the behavior of a large turbulent plasma cell that scintillates independently of other cells. The screens' spatial spread and varying distances from Earth were used to calculate the isotropic scattering measure at 1.77 kpc and estimate the size of the turbulent cell as 1.93 kpc, with a corresponding upper limit of 1.99 kpc. The study's findings have also led to a revised estimate of the pulsar's characteristic age and a more precise measurement of its rotation period. Additionally, the high-resolution scintillation data have provided a deeper understanding of the long-term variability of the pulsar's surrounding interstellar medium and the stability of the screen distribution over two decades. Further analysis of the data revealed a previously undetected, large-scale structure in the line of sight to the pulsar, with a size of approximately 1.5 kpc and a mass of 10 to the power of 31 grams, shaped like a dense cloud that is likely influenced by the pulsar but may also be a pre-existing large halo neutron star that is no longer radiating. The research has demonstrated the value of high-precision pulsar scintillation observations in revealing the intricate details of the surrounding interstellar medium, especially within the cells that scintillate independently of other cells, and has paved the way for future studies using more advanced radio telescopes. reconcile its key components with the cascaded network structure, which we
term "segmental architecture." We find that this architecture mimics the

approximation. As a result, we gain a more in-depth understanding of why the
TDCNC model performs better and how it can be further improved. Furthermore,

models featuring nonlinear activations and cascaded structures, including
ResNets and DenseNets. Interestingly, we find that these models can be transformed
into equivalent forms utilizing piecewise-linear components, thereby
deducing their predictive capabilities for quasi-periodic data. To validate our
analysis, we conduct comprehensive experiments across multiple speech classification
tasks, demonstrating the superiority of the TDCNN model and its counterparts
featuring the segmental architecture, which cannot be achieved through regular
network architectures. We also investigate the segmental architecture's impact
on other cascaded networks, uncovering the underlying factors that influence the
effectiveness of such structures in modeling quasi-periodic data. We hope that
our research will contribute to a deeper comprehension of the segmental
architecture and its far-reaching implications for cascaded networks. System

VGG-SS, a comprehensive audio source reconstruction dataset, has been developed in conjunction with a corresponding VGG-based model called VGG-Net. VGG-SS surpasses the performance of existing methods on a benchmark task for audio source separation and reconstruction. It achieves this through a combination of several key innovations, including the incorporation of VGG-Net as a baseline and the introduction of VGG-SS to tackle multi-source reconstruction tasks. VGG-SS differs from other datasets that are focused solely on single-source separation, due in part to its large and diverse collection of 4,946 training samples, along with accompanying VGG-Net model releases. When compared to the widely used DNN baseline, VGG-Net exhibits superior performance on various source separation tasks, including both single- and multi-source reconstructions, and demonstrates a high level of scalability without a significant decrease in performance. The development of VGG-SS and VGG-Net was motivated by the limitations of current datasets and algorithms in accurately reconstructing complex audio scenes, a task that VGG-SS was designed to address with its large-scale dataset and corresponding VGG-Net model releases. We perform a linearized analysis of an f(R) gravity theory, where the inclusion of a mass term in gravitational perturbations is considered a degree of freedom. Our study indicates that, due to the presence of an auxiliary field, the true degrees of freedom in the theory are more complex than previously believed. As a result, the inclusion of a mass term in the gravitational perturbations results in a false degree of freedom and ultimately leads to the banishment of this mass term as a linearized phenomenon. Our research paves the way for further exploration into the inclusion of a mass term in higher-order derivatives and its implications for the theory's stability. Additionally, an f(R) gravity theory with a mass term can be equivalently transformed into a second-order derivative theory with a ghost field, presenting a novel perspective on this concept. Our study also reveals the conditions under which an f(R) gravity theory can be converted from an arbitrary to a physically acceptable form, ensuring that the theory remains free from ghosts and other instabilities. We examine the relationship between quantum equilibrium states and Hamiltonian dynamics within quantum spin systems, focusing on the conditions under which a Hamiltonian's dynamics generates an equilibrium state. We establish necessary conditions for a Hamiltonian to yield an equilibrium state through its associated dynamics, and we derive three sublattice equilibrium state criteria. Depending on the spin dimension, we find four categories of Hamiltonian dynamics: (I) generating sublattice equilibrium states in any dimension, (II) producing ferromagnetic equilibrium states in one dimension, (III) yielding antiferromagnetic equilibrium states in one dimension, and (IIl) failing to produce equilibrium states in higher dimensions. Our analysis also includes a discussion of the spin chain's dynamics and the resulting equilibrium states, including examples such as the Ising chain and Heisenberg chain. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between quantum inverse temperature and dynamics, demonstrating its continuity in the one-dimensional case. Our study in (II) reveals that a low quantum inverse temperature corresponds to antiparallel spin alignment, while high quantum inverse temperature yields antiferromagnetic spin alignment in one dimension. We also explore the connection between Hamiltonian dynamics and quantum thermostatistics, establishing conditions under which additivity, and under quantum conditions, quantum additivity of quantum states hold. Finally, we establish the connection between quantum dynamics and quantum temperature, showing its continuity in one-dimensional spin chains. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the interplay between Hamiltonian dynamics, quantum temperature, and additivity of quantum states within quantum spin systems. Our results also highlight the limitations of quantum thermostatistics in spin systems with multiple degrees of freedom. We believe our study will serve as a starting point for further investigating the relationship between Hamiltonian dynamics and quantum thermostatistics within quantum spin systems. Our research framework is applicable to a wide range of spin chain models, including but not limited to the XY chain, Heisenberg chain, Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick chain, and Dicke chain. Our findings on the spin lattice case can be found in the companion paper [27]. We would like to emphasize that our research focuses exclusively on quantum spin systems and does not address related issues found in other physical contexts, such as classical mechanics and field theory. We introduce an enhanced spin-orbit coupling theory that incorporates strong interactions and strong crystal field splitting in transition metal oxides. This approach, applicable to a wide range of compounds including 3d and 4d transition metal oxides, allows the effective spin-orbit coupling to adapt to varying levels of electron correlations and crystal field splitting. By integrating the fundamental characteristics of spin-orbit coupling, crystal field splitting, and interaction effects, we develop a two-component model that includes an intrinsic spin-orbit component and a ligand-induced component. The effectiveness of this theory is demonstrated in a specific application to cuprates, and we highlight how the spin-orbit coupling can change sign in these materials. Furthermore, we show that the effective mass enhancement in these materials is directly proportional to the spin-orbit coupling mass enhancement. This is particularly notable when the spin-orbit coupling change is small, where the superconducting gap ratio can be explained by the mass enhancement effect. This new understanding of spin-orbit coupling in cuprates provides a compelling framework for understanding their unique electronic properties and phase transitions. This includes the Meissner effect, mass enhancement, and resulting $d$-wave symmetry of the superconducting gap, as well as the occurrence of charge ordering in some Er-doped cuprates.
